title: 2012 AMC 10B Problem 14
statement: Two equilateral triangles are contained in a square whose side length is \(2\sqrt 3.\) The bases of these triangles are opposite sides of the square, and their intersection is a rhombus. What is the area of the rhombus?

solutions.text:
This rhombus is created by placing two congruent equilateral triangles. Let the side length of it be \(s.\) Then, the area of one of them is \(\dfrac{s^2 \sqrt 3}4,\) making the total area \(\dfrac{s^2 \sqrt 3}2.\)

The side length of the larger equilateral triangle is \(2 \sqrt 3.\) The height of it is \(3\) since the height is equal to \(2 \sqrt 3 \sin(60^\circ) .\)

Half of the square is \(\sqrt 3,\) so the height of the smaller triangle is \(3 - \sqrt 3 .\) Thus, the ratio between \(s\) and \(2 \sqrt 3\) is \(\dfrac {3-\sqrt 3}3 .\)

As such, \[s = \dfrac{2 \sqrt 3(3-\sqrt 3)}3 = 2\sqrt 3-2 .\]

Therefore, the combined area is \[\begin{aligned} \dfrac{s^2 \sqrt 3}2 &= \dfrac{(2\sqrt 3-2)^2 \sqrt 3 }2 \\&= \dfrac{(16-8\sqrt 3) \sqrt 3 }2 \\&= 8 \sqrt 3 - 12 \end{aligned}\]

Thus, the correct answer is D .
hints: Use a \(30\)-\(60\)-\(90\) triangle near one corner of the square
Find one small triangle outside the rhombus and multiply its area by \(4\)
